blocks.text: 让我再试一次。

blocks.text: 这家史上增长最快的公司，拥有超过 1000 亿美元现金，很快将掌控价值数千亿美元的计算能力，有超过 11,000 家客户每年向它支付 10 万美元，它在告诉你，它要治愈癌症。在我看来，这听起来稍微合理了一点。

blocks.text: 三年来，我们通过铺天盖地的战略泄密、夸张吹嘘、FUD、关于虾福利的笑话、梗图，以及多得离谱的博客文章来了解 Anthropic。现在，我们终于通过它的 S-1 文件，拿到了冰冷、确凿、经 SEC 批准的数据。这份文件荒谬。离谱。愚蠢。它详细描述了一家资本主义历史上从未见过的企业。今天我会给你很多统计数据，但先从一个开头说起：Anthropic 自 2021 年成立以来已融资 1411 亿美元。截至 6 月 30 日，它仍持有 1317 亿美元现金及短期投资。也就是说，这家公司烧掉了不到 100 亿美元，就做到了单季 168 亿美元。而在那个季度，它甚至在经营层面实现了盈利。再说一次，荒谬。

blocks.text: 最让我印象深刻的是净收入留存率（NRR）。Anthropic 报告称，截至 9 月 30 日约为 900%。用 MBA 能听懂的话说：一年前付钱的客户，现在付的钱是原来的九倍。作为参照，任何上市软件公司公布过的最高 NRR 是 Snowflake 在 2019 年底的189%，当时其季度产品营收约为 6900 万美元。上市软件公司的中位数是110%。Anthropic 在 168 亿美元的季度上做到了 900%。再说一次，哎呀。

blocks.text: 话虽如此，不要过度看重这个数字。我认为基础模型更像好莱坞，而不是硅谷的 SaaS。在好莱坞，你只和你的下一部电影一样出色；在 LLM 这场游戏里，你只和你的下一个模型一样出色。他们今年增长九倍的原因是，Anthropic 在过去 12 个月里发布了一系列越来越强大的 Claude 模型（从 Opus 4.5 开始）。S-1 印证了我这个电影生意的心智模型。Anthropic 披露，发布超过六个月的模型贡献的收入不到 20%。截至 9 月 30 日的六个月内发布的版本贡献了第三季度超过 80% 的收入。所以前沿模型是一种半衰期为六个月的资产。随着模型本身越来越擅长制造新模型，我预计这个半衰期会随着时间推移而缩短。

blocks.text: 我的第二个证据是，这份文件多么清晰地展示了杰文斯悖论：随着 AI 变得更便宜、更高效，人们使用它的量大幅增加，以至于总支出上升。本质上，每次发布模型，更难的任务都必须变得更便宜，公司才能增长。该公司表示，每次发布都“将每项任务成本降低 25% 到 45%”。例如，在 2025 年 11 月 Opus 4.5 降价之后，环比增长从 48% 升至 132%。翻译过来就是：Anthropic 必须永远让用量增长快于降价速度，而其成本基础是提前数年锁定的。

blocks.text: 我的第三个电影逻辑证据是，Anthropic 的增长已经从荒谬放缓到仅仅是疯狂。第二季度环比增长 144%；第三季度约为 45%。部分原因是夏季，Fable 首次遭遇来自 OpenAI 和开放权重模型的真正竞争。部分原因是清理：该公司表示，5% 到 7% 的收入来自违反其使用政策的客户，主要是蒸馏 Claude 的实验室，公司在 8 月和 9 月切断了他们。（Opus 5.5 似乎至少部分恢复了增长曲线，但是否属实要看下一份财报。）

blocks.text: 到底是谁在付钱？

inlines.text: 到底是谁在付钱？

blocks.text: 尽管 S-1 开篇就提到 Anthropic 从事的是 AGI 业务，但就目前而言，Anthropic 主要做的是 Claude Code 业务。不使用 Claude Code 的 Claude Enterprise 用户每月花费不到 75 美元。使用它的前 5% 用户每月花费约 1,500 美元。这是关于 Anthropic 增长的最重要单一事实：这些模型恰好最擅长编程，公司自己在其上构建了应用层，并通过垂直整合的商业战略魔法，把价值留给了自己，而不是拱手让给 Cursor 和 Copilot。

blocks.text: 这是一门卖给几千家公司的使用型业务，而不是一门卖给4000万用户的软件业务。 S-1将企业客户定义为年付费10万美元以上的任何客户。按此定义，2025年收入的76%来自约1500家机构，其余24%来自合计约4000万客户。自推出以来，这一比例每年都保持在57%至90%之间。不妨把消费级产品更多看作漏斗和品牌。

blocks.text: 毛利率到底是什么？

inlines.text: 毛利率到底是什么？

blocks.text: 表面层面的分析师很可能会称赞Anthropic报告的85%毛利率。这将使该公司成为一只SaaS股票。然而，尽管公司使用的是SEC认可的定义，这一毛利率定义在精神上并不准确。

inlines.text: 表面层面的分析师很可能会称赞Anthropic报告的85%毛利率。这将使该公司成为一只SaaS股票。然而，尽管公司使用的是SEC认可的定义，这一毛利率定义在
精神上
并不准确。

blocks.text: 按报告口径，收入成本是归属于客户服务型工作负载的算力。但 Anthropic 在其自己的 IPO 文件中表示，它把算力作为一个可互换的池子来运行。客户今天购买的模型是六个月前用研究算力训练出来的，而训练它花费的数十亿美元在六个月后都将过时。因此，我认为要正确理解这家公司，就需要把前沿训练视为生产所售产品的成本。如果这样做，把总算力和基础设施支出都计入，那么销售成本就是 89 亿美元，毛利率为 45%。按这个数字，Anthropic 更像是一家硬件企业（这对它并不有利）。

blocks.text: 既然谈到利润表，就简要说明一下你会在每条头条新闻中看到的事实。Anthropic 在 2026 年上半年“亏损 807 亿美元”。这是一个毫无意义的数字，不值得担心。实际营业亏损为 6.93 亿美元。亏损是由亚马逊可转换票据的 724 亿美元按市值计价损失驱动的。这些票据在 IPO 时转换，因此上市后那个季度亏损就从损益表中消失了。（这是一种罕见的情况：800 亿美元的亏损可以很容易地被解读为买入信号。）

inlines.text: 算力支出荒谬至极

blocks.text: 当前算力支出约为每年 220 亿美元（按第二季度年化）。这些合同使明年的支出达到约每年 1200 亿美元，到 2028 年约为 1550 亿美元，其中大部分不可取消。与此同时，收入是按消费定价的，可随意取消，而且五大客户大多没有长期合同。长期债务与短期收入相结合，让我感到胃里翻腾。

blocks.text: S-1 文件花了大量篇幅论证这笔支出并非一笔好赌注。Anthropic 设计融资计划的方式，是将数据中心承诺（交付周期长、承担成本份额小）与加速器承诺（交付周期短、承担大部分成本）分开，这样最大的支票会在需求可见时更接近才开出。为支持这一计划，它又抛出了一个令人震惊的统计数据，即今年收入增长了 1,368%，而算力增长为 300%。此外，自 Claude 发布以来的每一个时期，需求都超过供应，因此公司实际经历过的风险是承诺不足，而非过度承诺。

blocks.text: For three years we have understood Anthropic through a deluge of strategic leaks, hyperbole, FUD, jokes about shrimp welfare, memes, and way, way too many blog posts. Now, finally, we have cold, hard, SEC-approved data, through its S-1 filing. This document is absurd. Ridiculous. Stupid. It gives the details on a business the likes of which we have never seen before in the history of capitalism. I’ll give you lots of statistics today, but to start off: Anthropic has raised $141.1 billion since its founding in 2021. As of June 30 it still had $131.7 billion in cash and short-term investments. So the company has burned through less than $10 billion to get to a $16.8 billion quarter. In said quarter, it was even profitable on an operating basis. Again, ridiculous.

blocks.text: Revenue increased from $376 million in Q1 2025 to $11.6 billion in Q2 2026. The third quarter of this year came in around $16.8 billion, though note that figure is press-reported; the S-1 leaves Q3 blank pending audit review. blocks.text: What impressed me most was net revenue retention (NRR). Anthropic reports it at approximately 900 percent as of September 30. In MBA-accessible English: The customers who were paying a year ago are now paying nine times as much. For context, the highest NRR any public software company has ever printed is Snowflake’s 189 percent in late 2019, on about $69 million of quarterly product revenue. The public software median is 110 percent. Anthropic did 900 percent on a $16.8 billion quarter. Again, yeesh.

blocks.text: That said, don’t over-index on this number. I think of foundation models as being akin to Hollywood, not Silicon Valley SaaS. In Tinseltown, you are only as good as your next movie, and in the LLM game, you are only as good as your next model. The reason they grew ninefold this year is because Anthropic released a series of ever-greater Claude models over the past 12 months (from Opus 4.5 onward). The S-1 backs up my movie business mental model. Anthropic disclosed that models older than six months earn less than 20 percent of revenue. Versions released in the six months up to September 30 produced more than 80 percent of Q3 revenue. So frontier models are an asset with a six-month half-life. As the models themselves get better at making new models, I would expect that half-life to decrease over time.

blocks.text: My second piece of evidence is how clearly the document illustrates Jevons paradox: As AI becomes cheaper and more efficient, people use so much more of it that total spending rises. Essentially, harder tasks have to cost less with each model release for the company to grow. The company says that every release “cuts cost per task 25 to 45%.” For example, after the Opus 4.5 price cut in November 2025, quarter-over-quarter growth went from 48 percent to 132 percent. Translation: Anthropic has to grow volume faster than it cuts price, forever, on a cost base that is contracted years in advance.

blocks.text: My third piece of movie logic evidence is that Anthropic’s growth is already slowing from absurd to merely insane. The second quarter was 144 percent quarter over quarter; the third was about 45 percent. Part of that is the summer, when Fable met real competition from OpenAI and open-weight models for the first time. Part of it is cleanup: The company says 5 to 7 percent of revenue came from customers violating its usage policy, mostly labs distilling Claude, and it cut them off in August and September. (Opus 5.5 appears to have at least partially restored the growth curve, but we’ll see in the next earnings if that is true.)

blocks.text: Who is actually paying?

inlines.text: Who is actually paying?

blocks.text: Despite starting off the S-1 with notes about how Anthropic is in the AGI business, for now, Anthropic is mostly in the Claude Code business. Claude Enterprise users who do not use Claude Code spend less than $75 a month. The top 5 percent of users, who do, spend about $1,500 a month. This is the single most important fact about Anthropic’s growth: The models happened to be the best at coding, the company built the application layer on top of them itself, and via the business strategy magic of vertical integration it captured the value instead of handing it to Cursor and Copilot.

blocks.text: This is a usage business sold to a few thousand companies, not a software company sold to 40 million users. The S-1 defines an enterprise customer as anyone paying $100,000 a year. By that definition, 76 percent of 2025 revenue came from about 1,500 organizations, and the other 24 percent came from roughly 40 million customers combined. The ratio has held between 57 percent and 90 percent every year since launch. Think of the consumer product more as a funnel and brand.

blocks.text: But the tiers are a power law. Each 10x step in annual spend cuts the customer count by about sevenfold, and the line extends cleanly to an implied 30 to 40 customers above $100 million a year. If you count every one of the 11,900 accounts at the bottom of its tier, the arithmetic floor is $5.15 billion. When you underwrite this company, you are underwriting roughly 250 relationships and the rate at which the next 1,650 climb into that group.

blocks.text: Despite that, the concentration risk is not the one in the risk factors. No single customer accounted for more than 10 percent of total revenue for the nine months prior to the filing. The top five were about 25 percent of revenue over the period, falling from 36 percent in Q1 to 21 percent in Q3 while each of the five set a record. That trend is the single best number for the bull case in the filing.

blocks.text: The problem is who the whales are. The reporting consensus is Cursor and GitHub Copilot, which the footnotes support in outline: Customers A and B were 12 percent each in 2025, and Customer C swung from 43 percent of revenue in 2023 to less than 10 percent to 11 percent in the first half of 2026. If that identification is right, the largest customers are coding products that sit between Anthropic and the end user, which have every incentive to route tokens to whichever model is cheapest this quarter, and whose owners (SpaceX and Microsoft, respectively) run their own model programs. The upside case is the mirror image. More than half the Fortune 500 pays Anthropic at least $100,000, and the filing says those companies spend less than 0.1 percent of their total expenses with it on average. The top 10 Fortune 500 accounts spend less than 1 percent. If the average Fortune 500 customer moved to where the top 10 already are, revenue from that cohort alone would grow eightfold. The bet at $2 trillion is that the power law keeps its shape while the whole curve shifts right.

blocks.text: Surface-level analysts will likely laud Anthropic’s reported 85 percent gross margin. This would make the company a SaaS stock. However, while the company is using the SEC-accepted definition, this gross margin definition isn’t spiritually accurate.

inlines.text: Surface-level analysts will likely laud Anthropic’s reported 85 percent gross margin. This would make the company a SaaS stock. However, while the company is using the SEC-accepted definition, this gross margin definition isn’t

blocks.text: Cost of revenue, as reported, is the compute attributed to customer-serving workloads. But Anthropic says, in its own IPO document, that it runs compute as one fungible pool. The model a customer is buying today was trained with research compute six months ago, and all the billions spent training it will be obsolete six months from now. So to properly understand this company, I think you need to treat frontier training as the cost of producing the thing being sold. If you do that by including total compute and infrastructure spend, then the cost of goods sold is $8.9 billion and gross margin is 45 percent. On that number, Anthropic is more akin to a hardware business (which is not to its benefit).

inlines.text: Cost of revenue, as reported, is the compute attributed to customer-serving workloads. But Anthropic says, in its own IPO document, that it runs compute as one fungible pool. The model a customer is buying today was trained with research compute six months ago, and all the billions spent training it will be obsolete six months from now. So to properly understand this company, I think you need to treat frontier training as the cost of producing the thing being sold. If you do that by including total compute and infrastructure spend, then the cost of goods sold is $8.9 billion and gross margin is 45 percent. On that number, Anthropic is more akin to a hardware business (which is not to its benefit).

blocks.text: Anthropic enjoys software gross margins when serving customers while suffering hardware gross margins when it does the research necessary to stay relevant. And as we’ve already established, the second cost never goes away. The closest comparison is the Netflix content-amortization debate from 2015 to 2019, when the argument was whether original programming should be expensed or capitalized over five years. Here the content expires in six months. Unfortunately, we don’t get much more detail on the future cost of training models—most likely because Anthropic doesn’t know what it’ll be well enough to publicly commit to something. But in my conversations with researchers, most of them expect the cost increase to be logarithmic.

blocks.text: While we’re on the income statement, a brief note on the fact you will see in every headline. Anthropic lost “$80.7 billion” in the first half of 2026. This is a nonsense number that isn’t worth worrying about. The actual operating loss was $693 million. The loss was driven by $72.4 billion of mark-to-market losses on Amazon’s convertible notes. The notes convert at the IPO, so the loss vanishes from the P&L the quarter after listing. (This is a rare case where an $80 billion loss could easily be interpreted as a buy signal.)

blocks.text: The compute spend is absurd

inlines.text: The compute spend is absurd

blocks.text: Current compute expense is about $22 billion a year, Q2 annualized. The contracts take that to roughly $120 billion a year next year and about $155 billion by 2028, most of it non-cancelable. Revenue, meanwhile, is consumption-priced and cancelable at will, and the five largest customers are mostly not on long-term contracts. Long-term debt being married to short-term revenue makes my stomach queasy.

blocks.text: The S-1 spends a lot of time arguing that this spend isn’t a good bet. Anthropic has structured the financing program such that it separates data-center commitments (which have long lead times and bear a small share of cost) from accelerator commitments (short lead times, most of the cost), so the biggest checks get written closer to when demand is visible. To back up this plan, it dropped another shocking statistic, namely that this year, revenue grew 1,368 percent against 300 percent growth in compute. Additionally, demand has exceeded supply in every single period since Claude launched, so the risk the company has actually lived through is under-commitment, not over-commitment.

blocks.text: So here is where we are. The most efficient scaling in the history of the industry, 900 percent net retention, 85 percent serving margins, $131 billion in the bank, and $800 billion of fixed obligations that the company can only meet if the next six models are as good as the last six. At $2 trillion, is that a buy? It depends, again, on whether you would trust Claude to cure cancer.
